claims.claim: Sendai virus induced MAVS aggregation, which was detected by semi-denaturing detergent agarose electrophoresis (SDD-AGE).
claims.source: In addition, Sendai virus also induced MAVS aggregation, which was detected by semi-denaturing detergent agarose electrophoresis (SDD-AGE; Figure 5—figure supplement 3D; Hou et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Bright MAVS puncta were observed in a majority of virus-infected cells showing clear p65 translocation.
claims.source: Based on the nuclear translocation of p65 after viral infection, these bright MAVS puncta were observed in a majority of virus-infected cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).

claims.claim: Bright puncta did not form in cells expressing MAVS mutants that failed to form filaments.
claims.source: In contrast, the bright puncta did not form in cells expressing MAVS mutants that failed to form filaments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, 2 and 3A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, 2, and 3A.

claims.claim: Mutants E80A and F16H that do not affect MAVS filament formation had normal puncta formation.
claims.source: As negative controls, mutants (E80A and F16H) that do not affect the MAVS filament formation were found to have normal puncta formation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, 2 and 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by imaging data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1, 2, and 3C.

claims.claim: The CARD-mediated aggregate formation is the key structural element for activating MAVS signaling in cells.
claims.source: Together these results support that the CARD-mediated aggregate formation is the key structural element for activating MAVS signaling in cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C,D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by multiple lines of experimental data.

claims.claim: SR-SIM increases both the lateral and axial resolutions by a factor of two compared to conventional fluorescence microscopy.
claims.source: SR-SIM increases both the lateral and axial resolutions by a factor of two (Gustafsson et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and cites a previous study (Gustafsson et al., 2008).

claims.claim: SR-SIM images of Flag-tagged wild-type MAVS showed a fairly uniform distribution on the surface of mitochondria in uninfected cells.
claims.source: SR-SIM images of Flag-tagged wild-type MAVS showed a fairly uniform distribution on the surface of mitochondria as it appeared in concentric rings around almost every MitoTracker-stained mitochondrion (Figure 5A, the last image in the top row).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in SR-SIM images in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: In cells infected with Sendai virus, SR-SIM images revealed a clear redistribution of MAVS into rod-shaped clusters that interfaced with only a small fraction of mitochondria.
claims.source: In cells infected with Sendai virus, the SR-SIM images revealed a clear redistribution of MAVS into rod-shaped clusters that interfaced with only a small fraction of mitochondria (e.g., white arrowheads in the rightmost image of the bottom row in Figure 5A).

claims.claim: The expression level of MAVS in cells remained the same before and after viral infection.
claims.source: Because the expression level of MAVS in cells remained the same before and after viral infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and references) (Hou et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013), the redistribution of MAVS from one mitochondrion to another during the puncta formation may result from mitochondrial fusion (Yasukawa et al., 2009; Castanier et al., 2010; Koshiba et al., 2011).

claims.claim: The redistribution of MAVS from one mitochondrion to another during puncta formation may result from mitochondrial fusion.
claims.source: Because the expression level of MAVS in cells remained the same before and after viral infection (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D and references) (Hou et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2013), the redistribution of MAVS from one mitochondrion to another during the puncta formation may result from mitochondrial fusion (Yasukawa et al., 2009; Castanier et al., 2010; Koshiba et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a possible explanation, supported by citations.

claims.claim: The diameter of the rod-shaped MAVS clusters is probably less than 100 nm.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and inferred from the resolution limit of SR-SIM.

claims.claim: MAVS aggregates were not evenly distributed around individual mitochondria, but were clustered into narrow regions on the surface of mitochondria.
claims.source: When a series of SR-SIM images were combined in IMARIS to reconstruct a 3D volume of MAVS and mitochondria in virus-infected cells (Figure 5B), it became clear that the MAVS aggregates were not evenly distributed around individual mitochondria, but were clustered into narrow regions on the surface of mitochondria (the rightmost image in Figure 5B).

claims.claim: Many rod-shaped MAVS clusters bridge between two or more mitochondrial membranes.
claims.source: Many of these rod-shaped clusters bridge between two or more mitochondrial membranes, suggesting that MAVS molecules from multiple mitochondria may contribute to the formation of one MAVS filament (magnified insets of Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in 3D reconstructions in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The mean filament length of MAVS clusters in virus-infected cells is approximately 400 nm.
claims.source: The mean filament length in the observed Poisson distribution is approximately 400 nm (full width at half maximum, or FWHM, n = 74) and the longer ones are ∼800 nm.

claims.claim: Each 400 nm MAVS filament contains approximately 720 MAVS molecules.
claims.source: Based on the cryoEM map, each 400 nm filament contains approximately 720 MAVS molecules.

claims.claim: After viral infection, activated MAVS molecules on the mitochondrial surface interact with each other at both the intra- and inter-strand interfaces between their CARD domains.

claims.claim: The CARD filaments form the central elements of the MAVS aggregates.

claims.claim: The filaments are localized on the mitochondrial surface and the MAVS TM domains are embedded inside the outer mitochondrial membranes.
claims.source: The filaments are localized on the mitochondrial surface and the MAVS TM domains are embedded inside the outer mitochondrial membranes.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by imaging data.

claims.claim: The spatial constraints provided by the CARD filament and mitochondrial membrane may force the intervening coiled sequence to be well extended and exposed for recruiting down-stream signaling molecules.
claims.source: These two ends of each MAVS molecule provide important spatial constraints that may force the intervening coiled sequence to be well extended and exposed for recruiting down-stream signaling molecules (Liu et al., 2013; Figure 6).

claims.claim: Bioinformatic analysis suggests that the middle segment of MAVS forms random coils.
claims.source: Bioinformatic analysis suggests that the middle segment of MAVS forms random coils, which, if present by themselves in aqueous phase, would not likely be fully extended and thus may deter efficient binding of multiple positive or negative regulators of MAVS.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The prion-like filament formation of MAVS uses very different chemistry than other prion proteins.
claims.source: The prion-like filament formation of MAVS thus uses very different chemistry than other prion proteins, and orchestrates the signaling domains of MAVS into a high-affinity platform for rapid and efficient signaling.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by structural analysis.

claims.claim: The filament formation of MAVS CARDs is based on collective interactions at the four interfaces of each subunit.

claims.claim: The four interfaces maintain the tight and dense packing of individual CARDs in the filaments.
claims.source: These interfaces maintain the tight and dense packing of individual CARDs in the filaments, which, together with the strong inter-strand electrostatic interactions, probably make the filaments detergent-resistant.

claims.claim: The strong inter-strand electrostatic interactions probably make the MAVS filaments detergent-resistant.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed explanation.

claims.claim: The net decrease in free energy supporting the filament formation is due to the four interaction interfaces for every CARD.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claims.claim: The counter-balance of positive and negative energy terms likely makes the MAVS filaments fairly sensitive to mutations.

claims.claim: The open ends of the CARD filaments provide three binding sites for each incoming CARD molecule.

claims.claim: Longer MAVS filaments are expected to be more stable than shorter ones due to the net gain in free energy for each CARD.

claims.claim: The physical length of MAVS filaments in cells may be limited by the number of MAVS molecules in each mitochondrion and by the dynamics of mitochondrial fusion and fission.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed explanation, supported by citations.

results.result: The authors determined cryo-EM structures of MAVS CARD and MAVS∆ProTM filaments at 9.6 Å and 16.4 Å resolution, respectively. Both structures are left-handed three-stranded helical filaments with specific helical parameters (azimuthal rotation ~53.6°, axial rise ~16.8 Å) and an ~18 Å central pore.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C10-C15 collectively describe the structural determination and key architectural features of MAVS filaments. The cryo-EM data (Figures 1 and 4), FSC analysis, cryo-ET validation of handedness, and measured helical parameters provide strong converging evidence for these structural claims.

results.result: The inter-strand interface in MAVS filaments is mediated primarily by electrostatic interactions between conserved charged residues (E26, R64, R65, and less conserved D23, R37). Point mutations at these positions abolish MAVS activity and filament formation without disrupting the CARD fold.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C18-C26 describe the inter-strand interface with structural modeling (Figure 2B), mutagenesis data showing loss of activity (Figure 2C), biochemical evidence of impaired filament formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and crystallographic confirmation that mutations don't alter the fold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Table 1). The evidence strongly supports the electrostatic nature of this interface.

results.result: The intra-strand interface is stabilized by hydrophobic interactions among ring-containing residues F16, W56, and Y30, with additional contributions from D53 and L48. Alanine substitutions abolish activity, but ring-containing substitutions rescue function, and mutations prevent CARD oligomerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C36 describe the intra-strand interface with structural modeling (Figure 3A), systematic mutagenesis showing loss and rescue of activity (Figure 3B), and gel filtration data confirming that mutations prevent oligomerization (Table 1). The rescue experiments with ring-containing residues provide particularly strong support for the hydrophobic packing mechanism.

results.result: Point mutations at both inter-strand and intra-strand interfaces impair MAVS filament formation and abolish antiviral signaling in cells, while control mutations outside these interfaces retain normal function. CARD-mediated aggregate formation is essential for MAVS signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C23-C24, C29, C52-C54 link structural interfaces to cellular function through multiple lines of evidence: luciferase reporter assays (Figures 2C, 3B), confocal imaging showing loss of puncta formation (Figure 5—figure supplements 1-2), SDD-AGE showing loss of aggregation (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D), and IFNβ induction assays (Figure 5—figure supplement 3C). The convergence of in vitro and cellular data strongly supports this result.

results.result: MAVS∆ProTM filaments have the same left-handed three-stranded CARD filament core as MAVS CARD alone, with additional peripheral densities ~15 Å away from the central filament. The CARD filament forms the organizational center with the rest of the molecule connected to its peripheral surface.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C45 describe the domain organization of near-full-length MAVS based on comparison of cryo-EM maps (Figure 4B-C). The overlapping central densities and similar helical parameters provide strong evidence that the CARD forms the core, with extra densities attributable to the intervening segment. This is a key architectural insight.

results.result: Super-resolution imaging of virus-infected cells reveals rod-shaped MAVS clusters (~400 nm mean length, containing ~720 molecules) on mitochondria that are not evenly distributed but clustered into narrow regions, often bridging between mitochondria. Viral infection induces redistribution of MAVS from uniform distribution to these rod-shaped clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C48-C51, C56-C57, C61-C64 describe MAVS organization in cells using SR-SIM imaging (Figure 5A-C). The data show clear redistribution upon infection, rod-shaped morphology, length distribution measurements (n=74), and 3D reconstructions showing bridging between mitochondria. The convergence of imaging modalities and quantification supports these cellular observations.

results.result: The first helix (H1) of MAVS CARD is not in direct contact with adjacent molecules in the filament, consistent with prior findings that N-terminal deletions don't impair filament formation. No cysteine pairs are at the interface, explaining resistance to reducing agents.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40 describe structural features with negative functional implications. The pseudoatomic model (Figure 1C, Video 2) shows H1 positioning, and these observations are consistent with prior experimental data (Hou et al., 2011) showing N-terminal deletions and DTT resistance. The structural model explains prior biochemical observations.

results.result: MAVS filaments could not be stained with Congo red and lack glutamine/asparagine-rich regions characteristic of β-sheet amyloid fibers, distinguishing them from classical prion structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C17 distinguish MAVS filaments from classical amyloids. The Congo red staining result cites prior work (Hou et al., 2011), and the sequence analysis is straightforward. This supports the conclusion that MAVS uses different chemistry than typical prions, though the negative result with Congo red could have alternative explanations.

results.result: Transient expression of wild-type MAVS results in constitutive signaling, but low expression levels in stable cell lines do not lead to constitutive activation of downstream target genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 describe the experimental system used for cellular studies. The transient expression observation cites multiple prior studies, and the stable cell line behavior is stated as an observation. This is a methodological detail that validates the experimental approach.

results.result: MAVS expression levels remain constant before and after viral infection, and the redistribution during puncta formation may result from mitochondrial fusion.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by Western blot data (Figure 5—figure supplement 3D) and citations. However, C59 is explicitly speculative ('may result from'), citing mitochondrial fusion as one possible mechanism. The authors acknowledge alternative explanations (degradation) but consider it less likely. The mechanism of redistribution requires additional experimental validation.

results.result: The diameter of rod-shaped MAVS clusters is probably less than 100 nm, the lateral resolution limit of SR-SIM.
results.evaluation: Claim C60 is an inference based on the resolution limit of SR-SIM rather than direct measurement. While reasonable, the actual diameter could be determined by higher-resolution techniques (e.g., STED, STORM, or electron microscopy of cellular samples). This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

results.result: After viral infection, activated MAVS molecules interact through CARD domains to form filaments that serve as central organizational elements. The spatial constraints between the CARD filament and mitochondrial membrane may force the intervening segment to extend and expose binding sites for downstream signaling molecules.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 synthesize structural and cellular data into a mechanistic model (Figure 6). The CARD filament as organizational center is supported by the MAVS∆ProTM structure (C45, C66), and the spatial constraint hypothesis (C69) is a reasonable inference from the architecture, though the 'may force' language indicates this is a proposed mechanism requiring validation.

results.result: MAVS filament formation uses distinct chemistry from other prions, based on collective interactions at four interfaces per subunit. The tight packing and strong electrostatic interactions likely confer detergent resistance, but the energy balance makes filaments sensitive to mutations at hot spots.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C77 provide mechanistic interpretation of the structural and mutagenesis data. The four-interface model is directly supported by the structure (C72), the mutational sensitivity is demonstrated experimentally (C77), and the detergent resistance explanation (C74) is consistent with prior biochemical data. The bioinformatic analysis of the middle segment (C70) supports the functional model.

results.result: The open ends of CARD filaments provide three binding sites for incoming molecules. Longer filaments are expected to be more stable due to net free energy gain, but cellular filament length may be limited by MAVS abundance per mitochondrion and mitochondrial dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 provide thermodynamic and cellular context for filament assembly. C78 is a direct inference from the three-stranded structure, C79 is a thermodynamic prediction consistent with observed long filaments in vitro, and C80 reconciles the shorter cellular filaments (~400 nm vs. up to 10 μm in vitro) with biological constraints. The logic is sound though C79-C80 are theoretical predictions.

results.result: Initiation of MAVS filament formation requires at least two independent molecules. RIG-I tandem CARDs are constrained and less likely to initiate directly, but RIG-I/K63-polyubiquitin 4:4 oligomers or RIG-I/MDA5-RNA helical complexes may nucleate MAVS filaments.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is a reasonable inference from the three-stranded structure with separated CARD units. C82 is structural reasoning about RIG-I constraints. However, C83-C84 are speculative mechanisms ('may nucleate', 'may present') citing prior work but not directly tested here. The initiation mechanism requires experimental validation, and the authors acknowledge uncertainty about whether RIG-I acts as monomers, dimers, or oligomers.

results.result: MAVS filaments use different interfaces than MyDDosome and are much longer, providing greater signal amplification. TRAF2/TRAF3 trimers may bind MAVS filaments with enhanced avidity, boosting signaling efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C86 compare MAVS to MyDDosome based on structural analysis and citations. C87-C88 contrast the functional implications of longer MAVS filaments. C89 cites prior structural work on TRAFs, and C90 proposes an avidity-based mechanism ('may enhance'). The comparison is well-supported, though the TRAF binding mechanism (C90) is speculative.

results.result: MAVS redistribution on mitochondria and bridging between mitochondria result from filament formation. Filament growth requires bringing randomly distributed MAVS into proximity, and the self-promoting nature may drive nearly complete incorporation of MAVS into filaments.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 interpret the SR-SIM imaging data (Figure 5) in light of the structural model. The redistribution and bridging are directly observed (C91), and the mechanistic interpretations (C92-C94) are logical inferences from the filament structure and thermodynamics. The self-promoting model (C94) is consistent with the prion-like behavior.

results.result: MAVS filament organization on mitochondria is distinct from MyDDosome and β-amyloid prions. The virtually irreversible polymerization provides a highly sensitive, robust, digital immune response mechanism allowing defense against lethal infections.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C97 synthesize the structural and functional findings into broader conclusions. C95 is supported by structural comparisons throughout the paper. C96-C97 are interpretive conclusions about the biological significance of the prion-like mechanism. While the 'digital response' concept is somewhat speculative, it's a reasonable interpretation of the all-or-none polymerization behavior.

results.result: The Introduction provides established background on innate immunity, RIG-I/MDA5 activation mechanisms, MAVS structure and function, and prior knowledge that MAVS forms prion-like aggregates through its CARD domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C98-C124 summarize established knowledge from the literature, appropriately cited throughout. These provide context for the study but are not novel findings. The authors accurately represent prior work on viral RNA sensing, RLR activation, MAVS domain structure, and prion-like aggregation.

results.result: SR-SIM increases both lateral and axial resolutions by a factor of two compared to conventional fluorescence microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claim C55 describes the resolution improvement of SR-SIM, citing Gustafsson et al., 2008. This is an accurate description of the technique's capabilities and is relevant for interpreting the imaging data.
